pages.text: The Estate Newspaper

image.note: Cover: kids with a laptop and a printed paper on a balcony

pages.text: Contents. The First Edition / The Team / The Scoop / Truth or Kindness / A Different Front Page / The Edition That Mattered.

"Stop the presses!" shouted Itohan, though there were no presses to stop, only a laptop, a wobbly printer, and four friends squashed onto her balcony. "We are going to make a newspaper. A real one, for the whole estate." Nobody laughed. That was how the Tafiya Times began.

image.note: Kids crowded on a balcony around a laptop

pages.text: Itohan had read a newspaper at her grandmother's, all folded and important, and she had thought: why not us? Tafiya Estate was full of stories. The new puppy at number nine. The mango tree that dropped fruit on cars. The lift that broke every other week. Somebody ought to write it all down.

image.note: Itohan reading a folded newspaper, thinking

pages.text: So she called a meeting. Down came Ese from the flat upstairs, and Boma, and Wali, and they sat on the balcony with a plate of chin-chin and argued happily about what a newspaper needed. "News," said Itohan. "Pictures," said Boma. "Snacks," said Wali, with his mouth full. "The truth," said Ese. "All of the truth."

image.note: The team meeting with a plate of snacks

pages.text: That was Ese all over. Whatever popped into her head came straight out of her mouth, gap tooth and all, with no stop in between. It made her the bravest reporter on the team, and, sometimes, the most dangerous. "We will call it the Tafiya Times," said Itohan, "and I will be the editor." "What does an editor do?" asked Wali. "Decides," said Itohan. She liked the sound of that.

image.note: Ese talking brightly, the others listening

pages.text: They shared out the jobs. Boma would take photographs on his mother's phone. Wali would report on food, which mostly meant tasting it. Ese would be chief reporter, sniffing out the real stories. And Itohan would edit it all, and decide what went in, and what stayed out.

image.note: The team assigning roles on the balcony

pages.text: For a week they gathered news. Boma photographed the mango tree and the puppy. Wali reviewed the new suya spot by the gate, giving it nine stars out of ten, then eating the evidence. And Ese roamed the estate with a notebook, asking everybody everything, which is exactly what a reporter should do.

image.note: The kids gathering news around the estate

pages.text: "People tell me things," Ese said happily, "when I just ask." And they did. By Friday the Tafiya Times had a puppy story, a mango story, a suya review, and a small piece on Remigius the gateman's new cap. It was sweet. It was tidy. And Itohan, reading it over, felt something was missing. "It needs a big story," she said. "A real one."

image.note: Itohan frowning over the draft pages

pages.text: The big story found them the very next morning, when the lift broke down again. It was the fourth time that month. Old Baba Danladi was stuck between floors for twenty minutes, and half the estate stood in the lobby grumbling. "Somebody keeps breaking that lift," said a neighbour. "I would love to know who."

image.note: A crowd in the lobby, broken lift doors

pages.text: Ese's eyes lit up. A mystery! A real scoop! She was off at once, notebook out, asking questions of everyone: the neighbours, the cleaners, Remigius at the gate. "When does it break? Who was near it? What did you see?" By evening she came bursting back to Itohan, breathless. "I know who breaks the lift," she said. "And you will not believe it."

image.note: Ese rushing back, notebook waving

pages.text: It was Baba Danladi himself. Ese had worked it out. The old man could no longer manage the stairs with his heavy market baskets, and was too proud to say so. So he wedged the lift doors open with his walking stick to hold it while he loaded, basket by basket, slowly, and the old lift, held too long, kept breaking down. "He does not mean to," said Ese. "But it is him."

image.note: Baba Danladi wedging the lift with his stick, baskets around

pages.text: "That is the story!" cried Ese. "THE LIFT MYSTERY SOLVED. Front page. Everyone will read it." And she was right. It would be the biggest story the Tafiya Times had ever run. Itohan should have been thrilled. Instead she felt strange, and a little cold, and she could not say why. She took the notebook and read it twice.

image.note: Itohan holding the notebook, troubled

pages.text: She thought about Baba Danladi, who gave the estate children sweets at festival time and never forgot a name. She thought about the words on the front page: everyone would laugh, and point, and the proud old man would know that the whole estate knew. "We cannot print this," she said quietly. Ese's mouth fell open. "But it is TRUE."

image.note: Itohan and Ese disagreeing on the balcony

pages.text: "It is true," said Itohan. "But true is not the only thing that matters. If we print it, we shame a good man for being old and proud. That is not news. That is just being unkind, in bigger letters." Ese folded her arms. "So we print nothing? And the lift keeps breaking?" And that, Itohan realised, was the real problem to solve.

image.note: Ese with arms folded, Itohan thinking hard

pages.text: Itohan stayed up late, chewing her pencil, and by morning she had it. "We will run the story," she told the surprised team, "but a different story. Not who breaks the lift. Why the lift is not enough. An estate full of elders, and one old broken lift they cannot rely on. That is the real news. And nobody gets shamed."

image.note: Itohan sketching a new front page late at night

pages.text: So they wrote it together. WHY TAFIYA NEEDS A LIFT THAT WORKS, said the headline. Inside, they wrote, kindly and truly, that many older residents struggled with the stairs, that the lift broke too often, and that the estate committee should mend it, or fit a better one, before somebody was hurt. Ese wrote the sharpest lines. It felt, at last, like a real newspaper.

image.note: The team writing the new front page together

pages.text: Only one thing could go wrong now, and it did. On printing morning the old printer jammed, halfway through the very first copy, with a horrible crunch, and would print not one page more. Forty copies to make, and a machine that had eaten itself. Wali looked ready to cry into the chin-chin.

image.note: The jammed printer, crumpled paper, dismayed kids

pages.text: It was Ese, of course, who fixed it, by saying the obvious thing everyone else had missed. "My aunty prints her church notices at the shop by the gate. It costs a little. We have Wali's snack money." Wali groaned, then, bravely, handed over the tin. Heroes are made in strange moments.

image.note: Ese suggesting the print shop, Wali surrendering his tin

pages.text: So the first Tafiya Times was printed, properly, at the shop by the gate, forty crisp copies, and the team pushed one under every door in the block. Then they waited, hearts thumping, to see what the estate would say.

image.note: Kids slipping newspapers under doors

pages.text: The estate loved it. Neighbours who had grumbled for months now had their complaint in print, fair and clear, and they carried it, that very week, to the estate committee. And the committee, moved to act by forty crisp copies, agreed at last to mend the lift, and to fit a small bench inside for those who needed to rest.

image.note: Neighbours reading the paper, nodding

pages.text: Best of all, nobody ever knew about Baba Danladi and his walking stick, nobody but the team, who kept his secret like true reporters should. When the new lift was fixed, the old man rode it up with his baskets, easy as anything, and never knew how close he had come to the front page.

image.note: Baba Danladi riding the mended lift, content

pages.text: "So," said Ese, as they shared out the last of the chin-chin, "we told the truth and we were kind. I did not know you could do both at once." "That," said Itohan, feeling very much like an editor, "is the whole job." And she opened her notebook to plan the next edition, because in an estate full of stories, the news never stops.

image.note: The team celebrating with snacks, planning the next edition

pages.text: The Tafiya Times team. Itohan, the editor, who decides. Ese, chief reporter, who says exactly what she thinks. Boma on photographs, and Wali on snacks. Motto: tell the truth, and be kind, and if you can, do both at once.
